newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China sugar factories face sour year as prices dip.
newsitem.headline: China sugar factories face sour year as prices dip.

text.p: China's sugar factories face another year of losses as the domestic price dips, forcing cash-strapped mills to sell at low prices just for money to pay farmers for cane, sugar traders said on Wednesday.
Prices in the southern province of Guangxi, China's prime sugar producer, dipped this week to 3,950 yuan ($476) per tonne, ensuring another year of losses, traders said.
Forward prices for February and March sugar were around 3,800-3,900 yuan ($458-470) per tonne.
"The question now is how big the losses will be, instead of can we break even," said one China-based sugar trader.
The domestic price of sugar should be around 4,300 yuan ($518) for factories to break even.
"Most of Guangxi's 100 or so sugar factories are facing difficulties," a source at one of the province's factories told Reuters by telephone.
Prices have dropped on oversupply while production costs have risen and sugar users, avoiding purchases in anticipation of further drops, were offering no support to the prices, the traders said.
China's surfeit of imports in 1995, boosted by sugar smuggled into the country, had resulted in a large amount of sugar carried into 1996, said one senior Chinese trader.
China imported around 2.95 million tonnes of sugar in 1995, up 90.3 percent from the previous year.
The crushing season was now well under way, further pushing down prices, other sugar traders said.
Government measures to buy around 300,000 tonnes of sugar this summer had temporarily firmed domestic prices, but the situation had not lasted, one trader said.
Sugar users, such as soft-drink manufacturers, were now buying only small amounts for immediate use, anticipating further price drops.
Production costs for sugar factories had risen as coal prices increased, Hong Kong traders said. Factories also had to pay farmers up front for cane, which increases the burden, they said.
"The government has issued strict instructions that factories cannot issue IOUs to farmers for the cane they buy," said a senior sugar trader in Beijing.
This meant that factories were forced to sell sugar, sometimes at any price, just to raise cash to pay farmers.
Banks were not helping with loans to ease the crunch, traders said.
"The government will not extend loans to loss-making companies. Many sugar mills made losses last year and will make losses this year as well," said one Hong Kong-based trader.
Weak domestic sugar prices were expected to continue into the middle of February, a Beijing-based source said.
"If the government does not allow imports in the first half of 1997, then prices will gain," he said.
China's sugar output in January to November 1996 reached 4.97 million tonnes, up 16.5 percent compared to the same period last year, government figures show.
Official output is pegged at 6.53 million tonnes for 1996.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
